To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we propose a method to learn the reward function by using a classifier trained with outcome data, 2) we show how to train a Bayesian classifier to make calibrated predictions, and 3) we show how this method is able to guide an RL agent to solve a number of challenging tasks.

1) a reward function can be learned automatically from outcome examples; 2) the resulting reward function is uncertain and must be interpreted in a calibrated manner; 3) uncertainty in the reward function is a powerful signal for guiding exploration in the environment; 4) uncertainty in the rewards can be obtained using a novel amortized normalized maximum-likelihood technique.

(1) a reward function can be inferred from outcome examples, (2) uncertainty can be obtained in a computationally efficient manner, and (3) this can be used to guide an RL algorithm to an effective policy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of learning reward functions from examples of successful states in the reinforcement learning setting.
the problem of reinforcement learning in which we are given examples of successful outcomes.
a class of problems in reinforcement learning where we have access to examples of outcome states that are desirable.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our method, which is based on the idea of using Bayesian classifiers to provide reward information, can be used to solve challenging reinforcement learning problems that are difficult for other algorithms to solve.
the proposed method is a novel algorithm for solving a challenging class of reinforcement learning tasks.
the proposed algorithm can learn a variety of tasks with high success rate and low failure rate, and it is more efficient in terms of the number of steps required.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose to use amortized normalized maximum-likelihood (ANML) for reward inference, which is then used to provide reward guidance for reinforcement learning algorithms.
we show that reinforcement learning can be guided by a Bayesian classifier that makes uncertainty-aware predictions.

we propose a novel method for reward function estimation from data that is able to provide calibrated uncertainty and can be used for effective reward-guided reinforcement learning in challenging environments.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in many settings, reinforcement learning algorithms can learn effective skills using only examples of successful outcomes, and that this is possible with standard algorithms when combined with uncertainty aware reward inference.
uncertainty in the classifier can be used as a signal for exploration, leading to a more efficient and sample efficient algorithm.
, with a carefully designed uncertainty mechanism, reinforcement learning algorithms can be guided by outcome examples towards an effective solution.
